analogy.p: Imagine you want to find out who is in a crowd by checking each person. Adding acid first is like asking people who look similar to the person you are checking to leave, otherwise they would trigger the same alarm. Then silver nitrate acts as a lock that gives a coloured light for each halide, and barium chloride is a lock that only opens for sulfate. The analogy breaks down because the 'troublemakers' are chemically destroyed rather than simply removed: carbonate ions turn into carbon dioxide gas and water.

bullets: **Carbonates**: add dilute acid; if CO₂ is given off it turns **limewater milky**.
**Halides**: add **dilute nitric acid**, then **silver nitrate solution**; a precipitate forms (**white** chloride, **cream** bromide, **yellow** iodide).
**Sulfates**: add **dilute hydrochloric acid**, then **barium chloride solution**; a **white precipitate** of barium sulfate forms.
All three tests identify the **anion**; cation tests are separate.
This is **triple (separate science) content only**.
Usually examined on **Paper 2**, in 2 to 6 mark questions about identifying an unknown salt.
Link to: flame tests, sodium hydroxide test, and instrumental methods.
core.h: What the specification asks you to know (triple science)
core.p: AQA Chemistry (triple only) requires you to describe tests to identify the three negative ions (**anions**): **carbonates**, **halides** (chloride, bromide, iodide) and **sulfates**. You must know the reagents, the exact order in which they are used, the observations that give a positive result, and the reason each step is needed. You should also be able to write the ionic equations for the reactions and to combine anion tests with the cation tests (flame tests and sodium hydroxide) to identify an unknown salt completely.

bullets: Add **dilute hydrochloric acid** (or another dilute acid) to the sample.
**Effervescence** (bubbles of gas) shows a gas is being made.
Pass the gas through **limewater**: it turns **milky/cloudy** if the gas is **carbon dioxide**.
Ionic equation: CO₃²⁻(aq) + 2H⁺(aq) → CO₂(g) + H₂O(l).
Limewater reaction: Ca(OH)₂(aq) + CO₂(g) → CaCO₃(s) + H₂O(l); the solid CaCO₃ makes it milky.
If CO₂ is bubbled for a long time, the milkiness can **disappear again** as soluble calcium hydrogencarbonate forms.
Use a **delivery tube** into limewater so none of the gas escapes before testing.
Do not say 'turns white': limewater goes **milky or cloudy**.
core.p: Carbonates react with dilute acids to give a salt, water and **carbon dioxide gas**, so adding acid to a carbonate causes **fizzing (effervescence)**. The gas is identified by bubbling it through **limewater** (calcium hydroxide solution), which turns **milky (cloudy)** because insoluble calcium carbonate forms. It is the combination of fizzing and limewater going milky that proves carbonate, because other gases such as hydrogen also cause bubbles but do not turn limewater milky. This test works on a solid carbonate or a solution.

bullets: Add **dilute nitric acid** first, then **silver nitrate solution**.
**Chloride**: **white** precipitate of **silver chloride, AgCl**.
**Bromide**: **cream** precipitate of **silver bromide, AgBr**.
**Iodide**: **yellow** precipitate of **silver iodide, AgI**.
Ionic equation: Ag⁺(aq) + X⁻(aq) → AgX(s), where X is Cl, Br or I.
Full equation example: NaCl(aq) + AgNO₃(aq) → AgCl(s) + NaNO₃(aq).
The colours get **darker** going down group 7 from chloride to iodide.
Silver fluoride is **soluble**, so no precipitate forms with fluoride.
core.h: Test for halide ions: reagents and results
core.p: The halide ions are chloride (Cl⁻), bromide (Br⁻) and iodide (I⁻). The reagent is **silver nitrate solution**, which gives **silver halide precipitates**. The precipitate is **white** for chloride, **cream** for bromide and **yellow** for iodide. The sample is first acidified with **dilute nitric acid**. The colour is the clue to which halide is present, so you must write the colour exactly: bromide's colour is cream (very pale yellow), so it is the one most often confused. Comparing the tubes side by side makes the difference clearer.

bullets: Purpose of the acid: to **remove carbonate (and hydroxide) ions** that would give a **false positive**.
Carbonate reacts with the acid to give **CO₂ and water**, so it is no longer present.
**Nitric acid** is used because **nitrate ions are spectators** and form no precipitate.
**Hydrochloric acid** would add **chloride ions**, giving a false white precipitate.
**Sulfuric acid** would add sulfate ions and give a false precipitate with silver ions.
This is a typical 'explain why' question: link **acid → removes carbonate → no false positive**.
If a question says 'why was the sample acidified?', say 'to remove carbonate ions'.
core.h: Why nitric acid is added first (halide test)
core.p: Silver ions form insoluble precipitates with other ions too, notably **carbonate** (silver carbonate) and **hydroxide**, which would look like a positive halide test. Adding **dilute nitric acid** first removes carbonate and hydroxide ions (carbonate is destroyed as CO₂ and water), so that only halide ions can give a precipitate with silver nitrate. Nitric acid is chosen because nitrate ions do not form a precipitate with silver ions. Hydrochloric acid cannot be used, because it contains chloride ions and would give a white precipitate itself, which would ruin the test.

bullets: Add **dilute hydrochloric acid** first, then **barium chloride solution**.
Positive result: a **white precipitate of barium sulfate, BaSO₄**.
Ionic equation: Ba²⁺(aq) + SO₄²⁻(aq) → BaSO₄(s).
Full equation example: Na₂SO₄(aq) + BaCl₂(aq) → BaSO₄(s) + 2NaCl(aq).
Acid is added to remove **carbonate ions**, which give a white **barium carbonate** precipitate.
**Hydrochloric acid** is used because chloride ions do not form a precipitate with barium ions.
**Sulfuric acid cannot be used**: it contains sulfate ions and would give a false positive.
If no precipitate forms, **sulfate is absent**; the solution stays clear.
core.p: Sulfate ions are identified by adding **dilute hydrochloric acid** followed by **barium chloride solution**. If sulfate is present, a **white precipitate of barium sulfate** forms. Barium sulfate is extremely insoluble, even in acid, so the precipitate remains. The acid is added first to remove carbonate ions, because barium ions would form a white precipitate of barium carbonate with carbonate, giving a false positive. Barium chloride (not barium nitrate or barium sulfate) is the standard AQA reagent.

bullets: **Halide test**: nitric acid then silver nitrate.
**Sulfate test**: hydrochloric acid then barium chloride.
**Carbonate test**: dilute acid and limewater; no precipitating reagent is needed.
Choose acids that **do not add the ion being tested for**.
Use **separate samples** of the unknown for each test.
Add the acid **before** the precipitating reagent, never after.
A **false positive** is a result suggesting an ion is present when it is not.
Describe in an exam: **'Add dilute nitric acid, then silver nitrate solution.'**
core.h: Why the order of reagents matters
core.p: The tests only work if each step is done in the correct order and with the correct acid. Adding the acid first changes unwanted ions into gas and water, leaving the ion you want to test for. Then adding the precipitating reagent gives a result you can trust. Mixing up the acids is the commonest mistake: nitric acid goes with silver nitrate (so no chloride or sulfate is added), while hydrochloric acid goes with barium chloride (so no sulfate is added and no silver or sulfate precipitates form). Always think: **what ions does my acid add?**

bullets: White → **chloride**, Cl⁻ (silver chloride).
Cream → **bromide**, Br⁻ (silver bromide).
Yellow → **iodide**, I⁻ (silver iodide).
The group 7 trend: precipitate colour becomes **darker** as you go down.
Use **known samples** side by side to judge the colour fairly.
Do not write 'pale yellow' as the colour for bromide: use **cream**.
The ions are in **solution**, so the compounds must be soluble (e.g. sodium halides) for the test to work.
Link to **group 7 reactivity**: displacement reactions between halogens and halides.
core.h: Colours and distinguishing the silver halides
core.p: The silver halide precipitates differ in colour, and the shade gets darker down the group. Chloride gives a white precipitate, bromide gives a cream precipitate and iodide gives a yellow precipitate. These colours are the evidence for the identity of the halide. Because cream can be hard to judge, a good answer says that the colours are compared, or that known samples are tested at the same time. Silver halides darken in light, but that is beyond GCSE. If a question gives a table of observations, match each colour to the ion carefully.

bullets: **Halide**: Ag⁺(aq) + Br⁻(aq) → AgBr(s) and Ag⁺(aq) + I⁻(aq) → AgI(s).
**Sulfate**: BaCl₂(aq) + Na₂SO₄(aq) → BaSO₄(s) + 2NaCl(aq).
**Carbonate**: Na₂CO₃(s) + 2HCl(aq) → 2NaCl(aq) + H₂O(l) + CO₂(g).
**Limewater**: Ca(OH)₂(aq) + CO₂(g) → CaCO₃(s) + H₂O(l).
Ionic equations contain **only the ions that react**: the rest are spectator ions.
Check **charge balance**: in CO₃²⁻ + 2H⁺ the charges cancel to give neutral products.
Always give **state symbols**: (aq), (s), (g), (l).
Formulae: silver nitrate is **AgNO₃**; barium chloride is **BaCl₂**; nitric acid is **HNO₃**.
core.p: Each test has an ionic equation that shows what is really happening: the ion being tested reacts with ions from the reagent and everything else is spectator. For halides: Ag⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq) → AgCl(s). For sulfates: Ba²⁺(aq) + SO₄²⁻(aq) → BaSO₄(s). For carbonates with acid: CO₃²⁻(aq) + 2H⁺(aq) → CO₂(g) + H₂O(l). Higher tier questions ask for these with state symbols and for the full balanced equation with a named salt. Use charges to get formulae right: Ag⁺ with NO₃⁻ gives AgNO₃, Ba²⁺ with Cl⁻ gives BaCl₂.

bullets: Use about **1 to 2 cm³** of sample in a clean test tube for each test.
Add **reagents dropwise** and shake gently; record observations.
Use **clean droppers** and tubes to avoid contamination.
Wear **eye protection**; **silver nitrate** stains skin and **barium compounds** are toxic.
For carbonate: use a **delivery tube** to limewater so the gas is tested.
Dispose of barium and silver waste **as instructed**, not down the sink.
Keep a **results table** listing test, observation and conclusion.
Use a **white background** to see pale precipitates.
core.p: Each test uses only a few cm³ of sample, so it is quick and cheap. Work with separate small samples, add reagents dropwise, and observe carefully. The reagents are hazardous: dilute acids are irritant, silver nitrate stains skin and is harmful to the eyes, and barium chloride solution is toxic if swallowed, so wear eye protection and wash hands. For gas tests, avoid sucking back limewater by removing the delivery tube before stopping heating.

bullets: Cation tests: **flame tests** and **sodium hydroxide precipitates**.
Anion tests: **carbonate, halide and sulfate** tests.
Name the compound as **cation + anion**: e.g. **copper sulfate**, **sodium chloride**.
Example: **lilac flame** + **yellow precipitate** = **potassium iodide**.
Example: **blue precipitate with NaOH** + **white precipitate with barium chloride** = **copper(II) sulfate**.
Do a test **table**: test, observation, ion identified.
If two ions could fit, say so and **suggest the next test**.
core.h: Combining anion and cation tests to identify a salt
core.p: An ionic compound contains a cation and an anion, so a complete identification needs both. Use a flame test or sodium hydroxide test to find the metal ion, and an anion test to find the negative ion. For example, a solid that gives a lilac flame (potassium) and a yellow precipitate with acidified silver nitrate is potassium iodide. State both ions and then the name of the compound. In an exam, link each observation to a conclusion and state the order of reagents clearly.

bullets: Chemical tests are **qualitative** and need **visible** changes.
Interfering ions can give **false positives**, so tests are done in a set order.
These tests cover only **three groups of anions**.
Instrumental methods are **fast, sensitive and accurate**.
Instrumental methods can use **very small samples** and identify **mixtures**.
Disadvantages: **expensive**, need **training**, and are not usually available in a school lab.
Evaluate in an exam: **speed and sensitivity versus cost**.
core.p: Chemical tests for ions are simple but have limits. They are **qualitative**, they need a reasonable amount of sample, and a mixture of ions can cause interfering results. Only carbonate, halide and sulfate anions are covered by these tests, so other anions, such as nitrate, need different tests. Instrumental methods such as **flame emission spectroscopy** are fast, sensitive and accurate for metal ions, and can detect tiny amounts and several ions at once, but the equipment is expensive and needs trained operators.

bullets: Use **mass = moles × Mr** and **moles = mass ÷ Mr**.
Moles of solution = **concentration (mol/dm³) × volume (dm³)**.
The ratio is **1 : 1** for Ba²⁺ : SO₄²⁻ and Ag⁺ : Cl⁻.
**Explain** answers: state the cause, e.g. 'barium carbonate would also be white', then the effect.
Check that the **final mass is reasonable** compared with the starting mass.
core.h: Higher tier style reasoning and calculations
core.p: Higher tier questions ask you to reason: why was acid added, what would happen without it, and what the result shows. They may also include a calculation of the mass of precipitate from moles. The pattern is: moles of ion (from mass or concentration × volume) → moles of precipitate using the equation ratio → mass using moles × Mr. For BaSO₄, Mr = 137 + 32 + 4 × 16 = 233. For AgCl, Mr = 108 + 35.5 = 143.5. Always check your units, and give an answer to appropriate significant figures.

bullets: **No fizzing with acid** means no carbonate; the limewater test is then not needed.
**Fizzing but limewater stays clear** means the gas is not carbon dioxide (it could be hydrogen from a metal).
If the sample is a **carbonate**, the nitric acid in the halide test destroys it, so no silver carbonate precipitate forms.
A precipitate with silver nitrate **without acid first** could be carbonate or hydroxide, not necessarily a halide.
A precipitate with barium chloride **without acid first** could be barium carbonate, so sulfate is not proved.
Record each result as **test, observation, conclusion** in a three-column table.
If two tests are positive, the sample contains **both** anions (a mixture); say so rather than choosing one.
core.h: Reading results tables and spotting false positives
core.p: Exam questions often give a table of observations and ask you to decide which ions are present. Treat each test separately and use a **fresh sample** each time, because adding one reagent changes the mixture. A positive result needs the exact observation named in the specification: **limewater turning milky**, a **white, cream or yellow precipitate** with acidified silver nitrate, or a **white precipitate** with barium chloride after hydrochloric acid. If the colour does not match, or no precipitate forms, the ion is not shown to be present. Think about what could give a **false positive** and say how the method prevents it.

bullets: Blue precipitate with NaOH and a white precipitate with BaCl₂ (after HCl): **copper(II) sulfate**.
Brown precipitate with NaOH and a white precipitate with acidified AgNO₃: **iron(III) chloride**.
Yellow flame and a cream precipitate with acidified AgNO₃: **sodium bromide**.
Orange-red flame, fizzing with acid and limewater milky: **calcium carbonate**.
White precipitate with NaOH that does not redissolve in excess, and a white precipitate with BaCl₂: **magnesium sulfate**.
Lilac flame and a yellow precipitate with acidified AgNO₃: **potassium iodide**.
Name format: **cation first, then anion** (sodium chloride, not chloride sodium).
core.h: Worked identifications: matching cation and anion results
core.p: Complete identification of a salt needs one cation result and one anion result. The AQA cation tests are flame tests (**lithium crimson, sodium yellow, potassium lilac, calcium orange-red, copper green**) and sodium hydroxide solution (**aluminium, calcium and magnesium white; copper(II) blue; iron(II) green; iron(III) brown**; the aluminium precipitate redissolves in excess). Combine the cation with the anion and write the name of the compound. Showing a link between each observation and the ion it proves is what earns the marks in 4 to 6 mark questions.

exam: Command word **'Describe a test'** (2 to 4 marks): give reagent, order, and positive result with colour.
For halides, write **'Add dilute nitric acid, then silver nitrate solution'** and give the colour for each halide.
For sulfate, write **'Add dilute hydrochloric acid, then barium chloride solution; white precipitate'**.
For carbonate, write **'Add dilute acid; bubble gas through limewater; it turns milky'**.
**'Why is the acid added first?'** → 'to remove carbonate ions / to avoid a false positive' (1 or 2 marks).
**'Why not use hydrochloric acid in the halide test?'** → 'it contains chloride ions, which would give a white precipitate'.
**'Write the ionic equation'** (2 to 3 marks): correct formulae, balanced charges, and **state symbols**.
For a 6 mark question, structure each ion as **test → result → conclusion** and finish with the compound's name.
Use data tables: tick each ion's result against each test; combine with flame test results.
For calculations, show **moles → ratio → mass** with Mr written out.
**Evaluate** instrumental methods: mention speed, sensitivity, accuracy and cost.
**Results table questions (3 to 6 marks):** for each test write the observation, then the ion it shows, and use the cation result to name the full compound.

mistakes.r: Use **dilute nitric acid**; hydrochloric acid adds chloride ions and gives a false white precipitate.
mistakes.w: Add hydrochloric acid before silver nitrate in the halide test.

mistakes.r: Use **dilute hydrochloric acid**; sulfuric acid contains sulfate ions.
mistakes.w: Add sulfuric acid before barium chloride.

mistakes.r: Silver bromide is a **cream** precipitate; iodide is **yellow**.
mistakes.w: Bromide gives a pale yellow precipitate.
Limewater turns white or clear when CO₂ is present.

mistakes.r: Acid is added to **remove carbonate ions**, which would give a false positive.
mistakes.w: The acid is added just to make the solution acidic.
The test for sulfate gives a coloured precipitate.

mistakes.r: Confirm with **limewater turning milky**; other gases also bubble.
mistakes.w: Bubbles mean the gas must be carbon dioxide.

mistakes.r: Barium chloride is **BaCl₂** and silver nitrate is **AgNO₃**.
mistakes.w: Ba(Cl) or AgNO for the reagents.

mistakes.r: Silver nitrate must be added after dilute nitric acid; on its own it can also precipitate carbonate or hydroxide.
mistakes.w: Silver nitrate alone is enough to show a halide.

mistakes.r: The precipitates are silver chloride, AgCl, silver bromide, AgBr and silver iodide, AgI.
mistakes.w: Calling the precipitates 'silver chlorine' or 'silver iodine'.

summary: You need to know the chemical tests for three anions: carbonates (acid, then CO₂ turns limewater milky), halides (dilute nitric acid then silver nitrate: white chloride, cream bromide, yellow iodide) and sulfates (dilute hydrochloric acid then barium chloride: white precipitate). It matters because you must explain the order of reagents and combine these with cation tests to identify an unknown salt in Paper 2. Required wording: the test for each anion, the order of reagents, the colour of each precipitate, and the reason acid is added first.

terms.d: A negatively charged ion, e.g. chloride, sulfate or carbonate.
A positively charged ion, e.g. a metal ion.

Bubbles of gas given off from a liquid, also called fizzing.
Calcium hydroxide solution, used to test for carbon dioxide; it turns milky.
AgNO₃(aq), the reagent used to test for halide ions.
BaCl₂(aq), the reagent used to test for sulfate ions.
A result that suggests an ion is present when it is not.
To add acid to a solution, here to remove carbonate ions before testing.
An ion present in a reaction that does not take part in it.
An equation showing only the ions that react and the substances formed.
A test that shows what is present but not how much.
An analysis using a machine, e.g. flame emission spectroscopy, which is fast, accurate and sensitive.
A compound made of positive and negative ions held together by electrostatic attraction, for example NaCl.

worked.ans: Potassium iodide, KI (iodide from the yellow silver iodide precipitate, potassium from the lilac flame).
worked.q: A solution gives a yellow precipitate when dilute nitric acid and then silver nitrate solution are added. A flame test on the solid gives a lilac flame. Name the compound. (3 marks)
steps: Yellow precipitate with acidified silver nitrate shows the anion is iodide, I⁻.
Lilac flame shows the cation is potassium, K⁺.
Combine the cation and anion to name the compound.

worked.ans: Add dilute hydrochloric acid, then barium chloride solution. A white precipitate of barium sulfate forms, showing sulfate ions are present: Ba²⁺(aq) + SO₄²⁻(aq) → BaSO₄(s). The acid is added first to remove carbonate ions, which would form white barium carbonate and give a false positive.
worked.q: Describe how you would show that a solution of sodium sulfate contains sulfate ions, and explain why hydrochloric acid is added first. (4 marks)
steps: Add dilute hydrochloric acid to the sample first.
A white precipitate of barium sulfate shows sulfate is present.
Acid removes carbonate ions that would also give a white precipitate with barium ions.

worked.q: 0.020 mol of sodium sulfate reacts with excess barium chloride solution. Calculate the mass of barium sulfate formed. (Ar: Ba = 137, S = 32, O = 16) (3 marks)
steps: Na₂SO₄ + BaCl₂ → BaSO₄ + 2NaCl, so moles of BaSO₄ = moles of Na₂SO₄ = 0.020 mol.
